title: when does “unseen data” stop being unseen?
author: AzimuthSystems
selftext:
been thinking about this a lot lately. say you keep a holdout set and never train on it, sounds clean. but then you test 20, 50, 100 different versions of the strategy and keep checking which one survives on that same holdout.

at some point you're basically optimizing against it even if you never directly trained on it.

how do you guys handle this in practice? new holdout every X experiments? track number of attempts? keep one final dataset nobody touches until the very end?

curious where people draw the line

comments.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
comments.body: I treat a holdout as spent once I've used it to choose between versions. After that it's validation data, not unseen data. With Anduril I kept selection and stress tests separate, then used one live session this week — 6 closed trades across 5 FX pairs, all green — as forward evidence, not proof. Still far too early to draw conclusions.

replies.author: AzimuthSystems
replies.body: yeah that makes sense. once you use the holdout to pick a version, it's not really unseen anymore. and 6 green trades is nice but yeah way too early to call anything. how are you deciding when a live sample is finally big enough to trust a bit more?

replies.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
replies.body: No magic number for me. I start trusting it more when the live sample has crossed a few different market regimes and the trade distribution still resembles the out-of-sample tests: expectancy, drawdown, holding time and costs, not just win rate. For Anduril I’d want a few hundred trades and several months before making any serious claim. Until then I’m checking whether the 21 modules behave as designed, not whether the PnL looks pretty.

replies.author: AzimuthSystems
replies.body: 21 modules is a lot lol. which ones have been giving you the most trouble in live testing so far?

replies.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
replies.body: The mean-reversion modules have been the most annoying so far, especially around regime shifts. A few can also lean into the same FX theme at once, so the portfolio layer sometimes has to reduce or skip exposure. The faster modules are more sensitive to spread and slippage too. Trend modules have behaved much cleaner live.

replies.author: AzimuthSystems
replies.body: yeah that tracks. mean reversion getting wrecked around regime shifts makes sense. are you detecting the regime change explicitly, or mostly noticing it after those modules start degrading?

replies.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
replies.body: Both, but I don’t let short-term live PnL make the decision. Each module has explicit volatility and trend-regime checks before entry. Live degradation is a slower kill switch: if expectancy, drawdown or trade distribution drift outside the tested range over a meaningful sample, its weight is reduced or the module is paused. One bad patch alone isn’t enough.

replies.author: AzimuthSystems
replies.body: yeah that makes sense. i like the idea of treating live degradation as a slow kill switch instead of reacting to every bad patch. appreciate the explanation
